subject: telescope
pitch: A brass explorer's telescope on a wooden tripod. A long tube in polished brass with leather-wrapped sections and engraved rings, a smaller finder scope on top, an eyepiece with a rubber cup, focusing knobs, and a mahogany tripod with brass fittings and a little tray holding a rolled star chart.
reasoning:
I'm planning the telescope model's proportions—tripod legs around 0.8m, tube length 0.7m with a 0.05 radius—keeping it as simple non-jointed geometry since it's a prop, not a creature.

I'm setting up a root joint at the origin so parts can attach properly, then considering the SDK's part-building tools (rods, sweeps, lathes, extrusions) and painting techniques like grain and mottle for mahogany and leather textures. For the telescope tube itself, I'm working out how to tilt it along a diagonal axis and use banded color sections to simulate brass fittings and leather grip sections along its length.

I'm defining a helper function that builds cylinder segments aimed from one point to another, letting me construct the tube, spherical joints, and tripod legs by specifying start/end points and radii. I'm planning the tripod legs as wood-colored cylinders splaying out from a central hub, painted with a mahogany grain texture.

Setting up the joint hierarchy with a root "base" joint, then a "mount" joint at the hub height for parenting the tube parts, since props don't strictly need joints but it keeps the rig clean.

Now I'm laying out the tripod geometry: a hub at the top of the legs, three legs spaced 120 degrees apart with feet positioned radially outward at ground level, modeled as mahogany cylinders with brass ferrule shoes near the tips for detail.

I'm adding a brass collar at the hub and a wooden center column descending into the tripod head, then figuring out where to place a small brass-rimmed tray holding a rolled star chart partway down the legs, which requires computing the leg radius at that height using linear interpolation between the hub (radius 0) and the feet (radius 0.42).

I'll settle on a mahogany disc tray around y=.30 with a brass rim, supported by a central mahogany column running from y=.3 to y=.7, and a small rolled paper cylinder resting on top to represent the star chart. Now I'm moving on to placing the telescope itself at the hub.

For the telescope, I'll give it a brass yoke mount with a horizontal cross-pin for tilting, positioned at the hub top with the tube angled upward about 19 degrees. The main tube runs roughly 0.74 units long from a rear focuser housing to the front objective end, with a radius around .045, and I'm now detailing the rear focuser cap with knurled focusing knobs.

Writing more cylinder specs...

Computing the perpendicular offset vector for the finder scope so it sits parallel to the main tube but shifted up and forward, defining its tube start point from that offset.

I'm positioning the eyepiece assembly at the rear end of the telescope, placing a brass barrel and rubber eye cup along the tube's axis direction.

Now I'm building the main tube as a single cylinder spanning between the two key points, with brass material under what should look like a leather-wrapped section.

For the leather bands, I'm adding slightly larger-radius cylinder segments around the body at intervals to simulate wrapped bands without complex sweep geometry. Then I'm roughing out the yoke mount: a brass cross-pin along the x-axis at the pivot point, with U-shaped bracket arms extending down from the pin ends toward the tripod head, still working out proportions for the arm lengths and positions.

Checking visibility: since the pin runs along x through the tube's axis, it's hidden inside the tube except near the ends, which read visually as trunnions protruding on either side.

Now I'm sketching the saddle standards as short brass cylinders connecting the hub top to the pin height, then working out the tripod legs — a mahogany head cylinder at the hub, with legs splaying outward from the hub center down to feet positioned in a circle at the base, giving a realistic tripod spread angle.

Tapering the leg cylinders so they're thicker near the hub and thinner at the feet, adding brass ferrules near the foot ends oriented along each leg's axis, and applying mahogany wood grain texture to the legs using world-space orientation. Now I'm positioning a tray partway up the center column.

For the tray, I'm creating a mahogany disc with a thin brass torus rim laid flat around its edge, with the central column running from the hub down to the tray's top surface. Then I start sketching a rolled star chart as a small paper-textured cylinder.

I'm also considering adding a leather strap ring and a small flat chart slab with an SVG star texture on the tray for visual detail, positioning them with care so the plane geometry lies flat and faces the right direction.

I'll simplify and just include the rolled chart alongside a flat sheet underneath, skip the extra bonus card, and keep a paper cap. For the telescope I'll finalize the mahogany and brass palette with engraved leather sections, adding small brass tori rings around the tube at a few points along its length.

Now I'm positioning the finder scope as a small offset cylinder with mounting brackets attached via thin vertical struts, plus a dark front glass disc. I'm also placing two knurled focuser knobs on either side of the rear tube section, sized to sit just outside the tube's radius.

For the rear assembly, I'm defining the eyepiece barrel and rubber eyecup as stacked cylinders extending backward from the rear cap point. Then I'm setting up vector math helper functions to construct cylinders between two points with configurable radii at each end, making sure the geometry orientation matches the aim direction correctly.

I'm also planning the joint hierarchy—base, head, and scope—so legs attach to the base, the tube attaches to a scope joint parented under head, with explicit bone assignments for each part to keep everything rigid and properly named.

For materials, I'm defining reusable paint constants: a wood grain texture in dark browns, a mottled leather texture, solid brass tones for metal parts with a darker engraved ring variant, plus flat colors for rubber and glass components, keeping the paint sheet packing efficient across the small parts.

For the star chart texture, I'm generating an SVG with a dark blue background and scattered star circles using the SDK's rng helper, then converting it to a pixel texture sized for a plane geometry with proper UV mapping.

Now I'm working out the tube geometry: the main brass tube runs between two points offset along the device's axis, with leather bands as slightly larger-radius cylinders and brass rings as toruses positioned at parameterized points along that length.

Mapping out the sections more precisely now: main brass cylinder with a thicker rear focuser overlay, leather wrap bands at specific intervals with mottled coloring, thin brass rings positioned near the leather edges, and an objective cell collar plus glass disc near the front end. Still writing geometry placement...

Now I'm working out the mount hardware — a yoke pin through the standards, a mahogany head cylinder with a brass cap disc, and three legs splayed at even angular intervals around the tripod base, with one leg oriented toward the front of the model.

Each leg tapers from a wider radius at the head to narrower at the foot, with a brass collar at the head/leg junction and a ferrule plus small rubber-tipped sphere near each foot. I'm also adding a central mahogany column running partway down from the head to meet a tray below.

The tray is a mahogany disc held centrally by the column, positioned so the legs pass outside its radius, with a brass rim detail. On the tray, I'm placing a rolled star chart as a small cylinder with a leather strap wrapped around its center.

A flat chart plane sits adjacent on the tray, sized and positioned so it doesn't overlap the rolled chart, oriented upward with its texture mapped to lie flat against the tray surface. I'm checking the dimensions carefully to make sure both chart pieces fit within the tray's radius without clipping outside its edge.

Now I'm working out the finder scope geometry — a brass tube running along the vector from the mount point outward, with support bracket cylinders and torus-shaped clamp rings securing it at specific offsets along its axis.

Shifting to the eyepiece assembly: I'm placing a brass barrel at the rear of the focuser tube, adding a rubber eyecup cylinder with a small rim torus, then positioning the focus knobs as paired discs with knurled brass shafts extending outward along the x-axis on either side of the tube.

Now I'm working out the stand -- making sure the legs, feet, and shoe spheres all sit flush with the ground at y=0 so the whole telescope stands properly without sinking or floating.

With the overall assembly roughly 1.12m tall, close to a real tripod-mounted telescope, I'm now sketching out the paint sheet for wood, brass, and leather parts, then setting up the exported meta object and the builder function with its joints for base, head, and scope hierarchy.

Writing cylinder helper function...

Plane geometry accepts a dir array too, for things like chart textures. I'm double-checking the paint types and imports — making sure grain, mottle, svg, and the THREE namespace are all properly exported and imported.

Now I'm sketching out the telescope model: brass tube and finder scope, leather-wrapped sections, rubber eyepiece, glass lens color, and a mahogany tripod with a star-chart paper tray, defining the color palette and starting the builder setup.

Writing the model code...

Adding the focuser housing, objective collar, leather grip bands, and engraved brass rings along the barrel...

Positioning the focus knob shafts relative to the axis point, making sure they're inside the housing radius and the knob disc spans correctly around the shaft end.

For the eyepiece, I'm placing a brass barrel outward from point A, then adding a rubber eyecup further out with a dark end-cap disc to give it a hollow, shadowed look. Next I'm starting the finder scope geometry, computing a new anchor point offset from the main tube along its normal.

Now I'm adding the finder scope's details: the brass tube body, a dark front rim ring, a glass front disc, and a rear rubber eyecup, then attaching mounting brackets with clamp rings at two points along the tube that connect the finder to the main body while checking that they properly bridge the gap between the two surfaces.

I'm turning to the mount yoke itself, building the horizontal pin that passes through the head and the two vertical standards positioned symmetrically on either side, then shaping the wooden head cylinder with a brass top cap and collar to finish the joint where everything connects.

Now I'm constructing the column and tripod legs - a central wooden column rising from the base, three legs splayed out at 120-degree intervals with brass ferrules near the feet and rubber sphere tips for grip. I'm checking that the leg spread radius doesn't conflict with where the telescope tube extends forward.

Next I'm adding the accessory tray on the column: a wooden disc with a thin brass rim, plus a rolled star chart resting on it, complete with a ribbon tie and brass end caps on the paper roll.

For the flat star chart itself, I'm working out how a plane geometry oriented along the "up" axis maps its local coordinates into world space, so the printed texture faces correctly outward. Then I'm generating the chart texture as SVG markup, scattering randomized stars across it.

Writing SVG constellation lines...

I'm also sanity-checking naming conflicts between my helper functions (tube, disc, hoop, ball, chart) and the builder's own methods so nothing collides, before finalizing the root part to return.

Fixing the eyepiece barrel so it doesn't float in a gap — adjusting it to run from Ae(0.02) to Ae(-0.10) so it connects properly to the focuser, then adding a small brass collar cap near the rear eyepiece. Now double-checking the leg geometry's radius tapering along its height.
